model.name: Digital Signature / Proof
model.purpose: Record, for a host subject, the assertion of a digital signature or cryptographic proof - the binding to what was signed, the signer reference, the signing method and policy, and the verification evidence observed - together with the governance controls that keep that record accountable, correctable only by supersession, and disclosable in separable classes.
model.scope_statement: WM-XCT-034 is a format-neutral mixin attached to a host record (document, dataset, message, claim or asset). It holds the proof instance and its identity, the binding to the signed material, the signing method and pinned parameters, the signer and role references, the pinned signature/validation policy, trust-anchor set and jurisdictional regime, and the verification evidence reported by external validators (indications, validation report references, certificate and trust-path references, revocation and status evidence, time-stamp references). It further holds the governance plane over that record: state and supersession, controlled change to algorithm, key reference, trust anchor and policy, emergency compromise response, review and approval evidence, bounded exceptions with expiry and rollback, role separation, disclosure classification, and retention, legal-hold, preservation and tombstone references. The model records inputs, references and reported outcomes only. It never generates, holds or destroys key material, never performs signing or validation, never operates a CA, TSA or trusted list, never proofs identity, never evaluates or enforces authorization, never determines legal effect, and never stores an audit trail or executes deletion.
in_scope: The proof instance attached to a host subject: its identifier, the binding to the signed material or canonical projection, and its recorded governance state.
The signing method reference: algorithm or cryptosuite identifier, hash, format profile, and pinned method parameters.
Signer and role references held as pointers to an external identity model rather than copied identity attributes.

Verification evidence as reported: validation indication and sub-indication, validation report reference, certificate and trust-path references, revocation and status evidence references, and time-stamp references.
Pinned signature policy, validation policy, trust-anchor or trusted-list set, and jurisdictional trust-service regime with jurisdiction and effective interval.
Proof governance lifecycle: declaration, immutable correction by supersession, expiry, invalidation, bounded exception and rollback.
Governance controls: role separation, review and approval evidence, disclosure classification, retention and legal-hold binding, preservation obligation and tombstone references.
out_of_scope: Key generation, custody, activation, rotation, destruction and cryptographic module operation.
Execution of signing or proof generation.
Certification authority, time-stamp authority and trusted-list operation, including certificate issuance and revocation publication.
Identity proofing and assurance-level assignment for signers.
Execution of signature validation or any local recomputation of a cryptographic outcome.
Determination of legal effect of a signature, seal or time stamp in any jurisdiction.
Audit trail capture, storage, query and audit-record retention.
Physical deletion, backup expiry, and the lifecycle and content semantics of the host record.

boundary_notes.distinction: This model records key and credential references, cryptoperiod claims and compromise declarations by reference; generation, custody, activation, rotation and destruction of key material are performed and evidenced by the key model.

boundary_notes.neighbor: PKI and trust service operation (CA, TSA, trusted lists)
boundary_notes.distinction: Certificate issuance, revocation publication, time-stamp issuance and trusted-list maintenance are external; this model pins their outputs by reference and version and never asserts issuer state itself.

Validation is performed by an external validator against pinned constraints; this model records the pinned constraints, the reported indication and the validation report reference, and never derives or overrides an outcome.

Retention schedules, legal holds and physical disposition are authored and executed by the records authority's model; this model records bindings and, once disposition is reported, a tombstone reference.
Whether a signature or seal carries a given legal effect in a jurisdiction is decided outside this model; only pinned regime references with jurisdiction and effective interval are held.
The signed payload, its versions and its own lifecycle belong to the host model; this mixin governs only the proof record attached to it.
Audit capture and audit retention, and evaluation and enforcement of access grants, are external; this model stores disclosure classifications and audit-entry references only.

sources.title: ETSI EN 319 102-1 - Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Procedures for Creation and Validation of AdES Digital Signatures; Part 1: Creation and Validation
sources.relevance: Normative validation process, actors (signer, verifier, driving application, signature policy issuer), validation status indications and sub-indications, and signature augmentation. Direct PDF retrieval was refused by the fetch path used; version, title and scope were corroborated from the ETSI deliverable listing and European Commission DSS documentation.

sources.title: ETSI TS 119 172-1 - Electronic Signatures and Infrastructures (ESI); Signature Policies; Part 1: Building blocks and table of contents for human readable signature policy documents
sources.relevance: Defines signature policy, signature applicability rules as business or legal fitness rules distinct from technical validation constraints, and the signature policy issuer role that signs the policy document. Supports policy pinning and the separation of policy authorship from signing and verification.

sources.title: ETSI TS 119 511 - Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Policy and security requirements for trust service providers providing long-term preservation of digital signatures or general data using digital signature techniques
sources.relevance: Preservation service policy, preservation profile and preservation evidence policy describing how preservation evidence is created and validated; supports the long-term evidence preservation obligation while keeping preservation service operation external.

sources.title: Verifiable Credential Data Integrity 1.0
sources.relevance: Proof as an attachable object with created and expires, verificationMethod, proof sets and ordered proof chains via id and previousProof, date-based cryptosuite versioning for algorithm agility, and the distinction between verification-method expiry (key compromise) and credential status (privilege loss), including privacy considerations about timing disclosure.

sources.title: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification
sources.organization: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
sources.relevance: Claim signatures over host assets, X.509 signer credentials with a claim-signing EKU, validator-configured and default trust lists, RFC 3161 time-stamps that keep manifests valid after credential expiry, validation status codes at error/warning/informational levels, and correction by appended update manifests rather than in-place edit.

sources.title: RFC 5280 - Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
sources.relevance: Certificate validity periods, CRL revocation reason codes including keyCompromise, cACompromise and superseded, the invalidityDate extension asserting when a private key was compromised, trust anchors, and certification path validation inputs including current time.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5: Recommendation for Key Management - Part 1: General
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Cryptoperiods, originator-usage and recipient-usage periods, key compromise handling, and authorization, access control and accountability frameworks for key management roles - the basis for treating key custody and compromise declaration as external inputs to this model.

sources.title: FIPS 186-5: Digital Signature Standard (DSS)
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Approved digital signature algorithm suite and the stated purposes of digital signatures - detecting unauthorized modification, authenticating the signatory, and non-repudiation - anchoring the method identifier and its intended assurance claims. A published errata notice means pinned algorithm identifiers should record the errata state.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-131A Revision 3 (Initial Public Draft): Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Algorithm transition governance: discontinuing DSA for signature generation, scheduled retirement of SHA-1 and 224-bit hash functions, transition from 112-bit to 128-bit security strength and to quantum-resistant algorithms. Draft status means transition dates are pinned by reference, not asserted.

sources.title: NARA Bulletin 2015-03: Guidance on Managing Digital Identity Authentication Records
sources.organization: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
sources.relevance: Requires documenting how overwritten or expired certificates are managed, keeping records authentic, reliable and usable for their full life cycle, retaining digital identity authentication records as long as the business records they support, and removing authentication measures that impede access before archival transfer.

sources.title: Records Management Guidance for Agencies Implementing Electronic Signature Technologies
sources.organization: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
sources.relevance: Enumerates the contextual records that must be retained to revalidate a signature later - certificates, the CRL current at signing, trust paths, trust verification records, certificate policies and practice statements, and algorithm details - plus the trustworthiness qualities of reliability, authenticity, integrity and usability. Marked superseded; used for the evidence-set enumeration, not for current US federal obligations.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 on electronic identification and trust services for electronic transactions in the internal market and repealing Directive 1999/93/EC (eIDAS)
sources.organization: legislation.gov.uk (UK-retained revised text), original: European Parliament and Council
sources.version_or_date: Revised text as at 3 September 2026, with pending UK amendments
sources.relevance: Article structure for jurisdictional regime pinning: Art. 22 trusted list, Art. 25 legal effects of electronic signatures, Art. 26 advanced signature requirements, Art. 32 validation of qualified electronic signatures, Art. 33 qualified validation service, Art. 34 qualified preservation service, Art. 35-40 seals, Art. 41-42 time stamps. The UK-retained revised text diverges from the EU consolidated text, evidencing why regime references must carry jurisdiction and effective interval.

sources.title: Baseline Requirements for the Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Code Signing Certificates
sources.version_or_date: Version 3.11, adopted by ballot CSCWG-32, 16 June 2026
sources.relevance: Industry-normative separation of subscriber key protection from CA operation, obligations to report suspected key compromise, bounded revocation investigation and action timelines, and the role of time-stamping in signature validity after certificate expiry or revocation. Binds publicly trusted code-signing CAs only.

sources.title: Digital Signature Service (DSS) Documentation
sources.organization: European Commission, DG DIGIT - Digital Building Blocks
sources.relevance: First-party technical documentation of the EU reference implementation: XML validation policy constraints, the ETSI EN 319 102-1 indications TOTAL-PASSED, TOTAL-FAILED and INDETERMINATE with sub-indications, augmentation levels B-B, B-T, B-LT and B-LTA, trusted list processing per TS 119 612 including status histories, validation reports per TS 119 102-2, and revocation freshness constraints.

sources.title: Universal Electronic Records Management (ERM) Requirements
sources.organization: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
sources.relevance: Lifecycle-phase requirements covering capture, metadata, maintenance, transfer and disposal for born-digital and digitized records, separating program requirements from system requirements - the basis for treating retention schedules, transfer and disposal execution as an external records model this mixin only binds to.

bundles.name: Proof Lifecycle, Controlled Change and Compromise Response
bundles.description: How a governed proof record comes into being, how it may only be corrected forward by supersession, how changes to algorithm, key reference, trust anchor and pinned policy are recorded, and how emergency compromise is captured, bounded by exceptions with mandatory expiry and defined rollback.
bundles.rationale: Every cited normative source separates the immutable cryptographic fact from the mutable governance judgement about it. Data Integrity expresses correction by appended proof chains, C2PA by update manifests, and X.509 by a superseded revocation reason - none by in-place edit. Algorithm transition and compromise are the two forces that invalidate previously acceptable proofs, and both originate outside this model, so they must be recorded as referenced events with scope and reported outcome rather than executed here.

layers.name: Governance State and Immutable Correction
layers.description: The state a proof record holds in the governance plane, distinct from the cryptographic outcome reported by an external validator, and the append-only supersession mechanism that is the only route to substantive correction.

findings.name: Governance state and its separation from reported validation outcome
findings.description: A proof record carries a governance state set by an accountable role - for example declared, in force, superseded, expired by policy, invalidated by compromise, or withdrawn. This is categorically not the cryptographic validation outcome. Validation indications such as TOTAL-PASSED, TOTAL-FAILED or INDETERMINATE with sub-indications, C2PA error, warning and informational status codes, or a Data Integrity verification result, are recorded as attributed observations from an external validator at a stated time, never recomputed or overridden here. A record may simultaneously hold an in-force governance state and an INDETERMINATE reported outcome; the model must be able to express that without collapsing the two.

questions.text: Which governance states may a proof record occupy, and which state transitions are permitted?
answer_data: Enumerated governance state codes with the pinned vocabulary version

findings.inline_only_rationale: The governance state and the reported validation indication are field-level values carried on the mixin itself and on referenced external reports. No separate document is produced: the state vocabulary belongs to the owner package, and the validation report is authored and stored by the external validator, so materialising a local artifact here would duplicate a target-owned record and invite it being treated as evidence this model did not create.

findings.name: Immutable correction by supersession
findings.description: A proof record is never edited in place for substantive content. A correction is expressed by issuing a successor record that references the record it replaces and by moving the prior record to a superseded state while keeping it resolvable. This mirrors ordered proof chains linked by previousProof, C2PA update manifests that document modifications while preserving prior provenance, and the X.509 superseded revocation reason. The superseded record retains its original pins, its original reported outcomes and its own supersession links, so an evidentiary chain can be reconstructed at any past point.

layers.name: Controlled Change to Method, Keys, Trust Anchors and Policy
layers.description: Governed change records for the signing method and key reference used for future proofs, and for the pinned signature policy, validation policy, trust-anchor set and jurisdictional regime that govern existing proofs.

findings.name: Controlled change of signing method and key reference
findings.description: Records a governed change to the algorithm or cryptosuite identifier, hash, format profile, or the key or signing-service reference used for proofs created after the change. Each method identifier carries a transition status drawn from the cryptographic transition regime - broadly acceptable, deprecated, restricted to verification of previously generated signatures, or disallowed - together with the effective interval of that status. A transition imposes remediation obligations on already recorded proofs: re-sign under a current method, augment with long-term validation material and archive time-stamps, or accept as legacy verification-only. Key generation, custody and rotation execution belong to the cryptographic key model; only the reference and the change record are held here.

Effective interval over which that status holds

findings.name: Trust-anchor set, signature policy and jurisdictional regime pinning
findings.description: Pins, by reference and version, the signature policy and validation policy that govern a proof, the trust-anchor or trusted-list set applicable at event time including the list's published version and status history, and any jurisdictional trust-service regime asserted to apply, with a jurisdiction code and an effective interval. Signature policies are authored and signed by a signature policy issuer and may contain applicability rules about business or legal fitness that go beyond technical validation constraints; this model pins them and never authors them. A pinned regime reference records that a regime was asserted, not that a legal conclusion holds.

layers.name: Compromise Response and Bounded Exceptions
layers.description: Emergency response to an externally declared compromise affecting proofs, and the time-boxed exceptions under which a proof that does not satisfy its pinned policy may still be accepted for a stated purpose.

findings.name: Emergency compromise response record
findings.description: Captures the reference to an externally declared compromise of a key, credential, algorithm or trust anchor, the reason code, the asserted invalidity time from which affected proofs are treated as suspect, the frozen set of proof records within the blast radius, the required response actions and the outcome reported by the executing party. Trusted time-stamps or a preserved long-term validation evidence set may mitigate the compromise for proofs demonstrably created before the invalidity time, so mitigation evidence is recorded alongside the scope. Revocation, key destruction, certificate reissuance and incident handling are executed by the key and PKI models under their own timelines; this model records the reference, the scope and the reported outcome.

findings.name: Bounded acceptance exceptions, expiry and rollback
findings.description: Records a time-boxed exception under which a proof that does not satisfy its pinned policy is nonetheless accepted for a stated and limited purpose - for example an INDETERMINATE outcome caused by unavailable revocation data, a stale revocation freshness constraint, or a method whose transition status has become verification-only. Every exception carries a mandatory expiry, a purpose limitation, a compensating condition, the approving authority and a defined rollback that restores the pre-exception governance state. An exception never alters the reported cryptographic outcome and never edits a pinned policy; it records a bounded governance tolerance of a known deficiency.

bundles.name: Accountability, Access Segregation and Evidentiary Retention
bundles.description: Who is accountable for what around a proof record, what evidences that governance decisions were reviewed, how the separable components of proof information are classified for disclosure, and how retention, legal hold, evidence preservation and tombstone references are bound to externally owned obligations.
bundles.rationale: Signature governance fails in two characteristic ways: one party silently accumulates signing authorization, key custody, verification-policy authority and legal-effect assessment; or public verifiability of a proof is taken to license access to the signed payload and the signer's identity attributes. Both failures are addressed by explicit role separation and independently classified disclosure. Retention is the third failure mode - a proof outlives the system that made it, so the evidence needed to revalidate it must be preserved by reference while disposition stays with the records authority.

layers.name: Role Separation and Review Evidence
layers.description: The distinct accountable roles over a proof record, the combinations that must not be held by one party, and the documented review and approval that must precede a governance decision taking effect.

findings.name: Governance role separation and prohibited combinations
findings.description: Names the distinct accountable roles over a proof record and binds each to a party reference: responsible owner, signature-policy authority, signer or signing operator, verifier, trust administrator, cryptographic custodian, reviewer or auditor, records authority, and the external legal-effect assessor. The core prohibition is that no single party may simultaneously hold signing authorization, cryptographic key custody, verification-policy authority and legal-effect assessment for the same proof record. Where an adopting Dimension is too small to separate them, the conflict must be recorded explicitly with a compensating control rather than silently collapsed. Party identity attributes, credentials and authorization enforcement remain in the identity and access models.

findings.name: Separable disclosure classes for proof information
findings.description: Classifies the components of a proof record into independently governed disclosure classes: host content, signature or proof bytes, certificates and public keys, signer identity attributes, revocation and status evidence, and sensitive validation diagnostics. Public verifiability of a proof does not imply public access to the signed payload, and never implies access to signer identity attributes. Proof timing values and status endpoints can themselves leak information about a controller, so expiry and status references are classified in their own right. Diagnostics that reveal internal trust configuration, failure detail or scope lists are treated as sensitive by default. Each class is bound to an externally authored access policy; evaluation and enforcement occur in the access model.

A proof record commonly outlives the system that produced it, so the preservation obligation is stated by reference to a preservation profile rather than by local copying. owner_package_requirements: The adopting Dimension must designate a responsible owner for the WM-XCT-034 mixin package before any proof record is created; the owner is accountable for the record plane only and holds neither key custody nor signing authorization.

The owner package must declare and resolve the external models it binds to: cryptographic key and credential, PKI and trust service, identity and actor, records retention and disposition, access control, and audit.

The owner package must publish, with an effective interval and a version, the governance state vocabulary and permitted transitions, the disclosure class vocabulary, the substantive-field list that forces supersession, and the role separation rules it applies.
The owner package must name a records authority and a signature-policy authority as parties distinct from each other and from the signer, cryptographic custodian and reviewer.
The owner package must state which external party performs legal-effect assessment and record that this model never performs it.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Locally minted identifiers are namespaced under the adopting Dimension's URI plus the model path wm-xct-034, consistent with the registered navigation path NAV.XCT.SIG and domain tag XCT.SIG. Every locally minted identifier must resolve within that namespace. Identifiers issued by external authorities - certificate issuer and serial pairs, controlled identifier document URLs, verification method IRIs, trusted-list service identifiers, time-stamp token serials - are carried verbatim in their own namespace and must never be re-minted, re-prefixed or presented as locally governed.
registry_links: Registry entry vr.wm-xct-034 with model_id WM-XCT-034, entry_kind mixin, navigation path NAV.XCT.SIG and domain tag XCT.SIG.
Registered parent WM-XCT-006 must resolve before this mixin is instantiated; if it does not resolve, instantiation is blocked rather than defaulted.
Vocabulary registries for governance states, disclosure classes, supersession reasons, exception grounds and transition statuses must be registered with versions and effective intervals.

canonicalization_rules: The canonical form is the abstract record graph, not any serialization; JSON, YAML, Markdown, HTML, Git objects, MCP resources and MongoDB documents are projections that must round-trip the graph without adding meaning.

Any canonicalization applied for cryptographic purposes belongs to the referenced cryptosuite or signature format and is recorded as a pinned method parameter; this model neither defines nor performs canonicalization for signing or verification.
Code values, jurisdiction codes, role codes and status codes are compared case-sensitively against the vocabulary version pinned on the record, never against a later vocabulary version.
Timestamps are normalized to UTC for comparison while the originally recorded offset is retained verbatim, because the offset can itself be evidence of where and when an event occurred.
patch_rules: Proof records are append-only for substantive content; a substantive correction is expressed only as a successor record that supersedes the prior one, and never as an in-place edit.

In-place update is confined to the non-substantive field list published in the owner package - typically observation time, resolvable pointers and disclosure classification - and every such patch carries an acting role reference, a reason code and a recorded-at time in RFC 3339.
A patch may never retroactively change a pinned policy version, trust-anchor set version or method identifier; such a change requires a new pin record with its own effective interval.
A reported validation outcome is never edited or removed; a differing result is recorded as an additional attributed observation with its own reporter and time.
Withdrawal of a governance decision is a forward-only rollback record; the original decision record is retained and remains resolvable.
compatibility_rules: Adding a governance state, disclosure class, reason code or exception ground is backward compatible only if every existing code retains its meaning and every prior record remains resolvable and interpretable under its own pinned vocabulary version.
Removing a code, narrowing its meaning or re-pointing it is a breaking change that requires a new vocabulary version and explicit re-pinning; silent re-meaning is prohibited.
Alignments to external standards are versioned references; a revision of an external standard does not retroactively alter a previously recorded alignment, reported outcome or conformance statement.
A projection format change is non-breaking only if it preserves identifiers, ordering of supersession chains, timestamp offsets and disclosure classifications exactly.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier issued by the system of record for the proof or its host - for example the signing service's proof record identifier or the host repository's record key - used verbatim and never re-minted.

Governed global identifier or IRI from a normative registry or namespace - for example a controlled identifier document URL, a verification method IRI, an X.509 issuer-and-serial pair, or a trusted-list service identifier - used when no master-system identifier exists.

UUID or ULID minted by the adopting Dimension, used only when neither an authoritative master-system identifier nor a governed global identifier exists, and recorded together with the reason the higher tiers were unavailable.

A date, a timestamp, a content digest alone, a file path or a sequence number is never an identifier; a digest may be recorded as an integrity value and a sequence may be used in an artifact name, but neither establishes record identity.
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All time values use RFC 3339 with explicit seconds and an explicit numeric offset or Z; a value lacking an offset is rejected rather than assumed to be UTC. Event time - when signing, supersession, a compromise, an approval or a disposition actually occurred - is recorded separately from observation or ingestion time, which is when this model learned of it, and both are retained whenever they differ. Where a trusted time-stamp token exists, its asserted time is recorded as a third, source-attributed value with the issuing authority reference, and is never merged with either of the other two.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artifacts - supersession, method change, policy and anchor pin, compromise response, exception, review and approval, and tombstone records - are named as the owning scope or proof record identifier, plus the artifact kind, plus a zero-padded monotonic sequence. The sequence is unique per owning identifier and per artifact kind, is never reused after deletion or supersession, and never contains a date, a timestamp or any date-derived component. Non-serial registers and schedules hold one current instance per governed scope with a monotonic version counter, and superseded versions remain resolvable.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: Every artifact carries a digest with its named algorithm and an explicit statement of the byte range or canonical projection the digest covers, together with the reference to any externally reported validation outcome associated with it. This model stores digests, references and reported outcomes; it never recomputes a digest as proof, never asserts cryptographic verification, and never treats a locally computed digest as equivalent to an external validator's result.

policies: Separation of duty: no single party may simultaneously hold signing authorization, cryptographic key custody, verification-policy authority and legal-effect assessment for the same proof record. Where an adopting Dimension cannot separate them, the conflict is declared explicitly with a compensating control, an approving role and a re-evaluation point.

No local legal conclusion: a jurisdictional qualified-signature, seal or trust-service regime is recorded only as a pinned reference with a jurisdiction code and an effective interval. The model never derives, stores or exposes a legal-validity flag, and never presents a regional legal conclusion as a universal fact.

Record plane only: this model records inputs, references and reported outcomes. Key custody, cryptographic execution, CA, TSA and trusted-list operation, identity proofing, authorization evaluation and enforcement, audit-trail storage and deletion execution stay with their owning models and are never simulated locally.
Immutable correction: substantive change occurs by supersession. Superseded records remain resolvable with their original pins and reported outcomes for the period set by the records authority.

Disclosure independence: public verifiability of a proof confers no access to the host payload, to signer identity attributes or to sensitive validation diagnostics; each is classified and granted separately.

read: Read is scoped by disclosure class; a caller cleared for proof bytes and certificates is not thereby cleared for host content, signer identity attributes or sensitive validation diagnostics.

A read of a proof record must return its governance state together with its pinned method identifier, policy version, trust-anchor set version and any active exception, so a reported outcome is never consumed without the constraints it was produced under.
Sensitive validation diagnostics, frozen compromise scope lists and revocation investigation detail are refused by default and require an explicit, recorded grant.
A read of a tombstone returns only the retained identifier, supersession links, disposition reason, reported time and authority reference.
create: A proof record may be created only with a resolvable host subject reference, an identifier chosen by the stated identity priority with the tier used recorded, and an assigned responsible owner.
Creation must pin the method identifier, signature and validation policy references and trust-anchor set version applicable at event time; an unpinnable creation is rejected rather than defaulted.
Creation may not fabricate or infer a validation outcome; the reported outcome remains unset until an external validator reports one with an attribution and a time.
Creation of a governance artifact requires the acting role to hold the corresponding authority and, where the decision type requires it, an existing review and approval record.
update: Substantive fields are append-only; a substantive change is made by creating a superseding record that references the prior one, never by mutation.
Permitted in-place updates are limited to the published non-substantive field list and must carry an acting role reference, a reason code and a recorded-at time.
A reported validation outcome is never edited; a differing result is added as a further attributed observation, preserving the original.
A pinned policy version, trust-anchor set version or jurisdictional regime interval is changed only through a new pin record, never by updating the existing pin.
delete: This model executes no deletion. Records are retained under the retention schedule referenced from the records authority's schedule model; where no schedule resolves, the record is retained and flagged for the records authority rather than disposed of by default.

A legal hold or evidence-preservation reference suspends all disposition of the covered records. The suspension and its scope are recorded here; enforcement of the suspension is performed by the records model.

When disposition is executed by the owning records or storage model and reported back, this model writes a tombstone containing only the record identifier, its supersession links, the disposition reason code, the reported disposition time and the ordering authority reference. No payload, no proof bytes, no certificates, no signer identity attributes and no diagnostics are retained in a tombstone, and prior references continue to resolve to it.

Physical erasure, backup and replica expiry, audit-record retention and host-record deletion are executed and evidenced by the referenced records-retention, storage, audit and host models under the adopting Dimension's disposition policy; this model records only the binding, the reported outcome and the tombstone.

roles.name: Responsible owner
responsibilities: Accountable for the completeness, currency and correctness of the proof record on the record plane.
Approves the owner package, the published vocabularies and the declared external model bindings.
Holds no key material, performs no signing and does not approve exceptions to decisions they themselves made.

roles.name: Signature-policy authority
responsibilities: Issues and versions the signature policy and validation policy that are pinned to proof records, including applicability rules about business or legal fitness.
Declares the effective interval of each policy version and the conditions requiring re-pinning.
Does not operate signing or verification and does not hold key custody.

roles.name: Signer or signing operator

roles.name: Verifier
responsibilities: Obtains validation outcomes from an external validator and records the reported indication, sub-indication and validation report reference with attribution and time.
Records revocation and status evidence references and their freshness at the time of validation.
Does not set the governance state, does not grant exceptions and does not determine legal effect.

roles.name: Trust administrator
responsibilities: Maintains the trust-anchor and trusted-list references, their published versions and their status-history references used in pins.

roles.name: Cryptographic custodian
responsibilities: Controls key material in the external key model and supplies key and credential references, cryptoperiod claims and compromise declarations to this model.

Must not hold verification-policy authority, must not approve exceptions and must not assess legal effect.

roles.name: Reviewer or auditor
responsibilities: Independently reviews governance decisions and the evidence before them, recording competence and independence basis.
Records the decision code, conditions and any dissent, and the audit entry reference for reconciliation.
Must not review a decision they took, and does not own or operate the audit record store.

roles.name: Records authority
responsibilities: Owns retention schedules, issues and releases legal holds, and orders and executes disposition in the records model.
Reports disposition back so that a tombstone can be written here.
Determines how long superseded records and preserved evidence sets remain resolvable.

roles.name: Legal-effect assessor (external)
responsibilities: Determines, outside this model, whether a signature, seal or time stamp carries a given legal effect in a given jurisdiction and interval.
Supplies only a reference to that assessment, which is recorded as an attributed external conclusion.
Holds no signing authorization, no key custody and no verification-policy authority.

access.default_rule: Deny by default at every scope. A caller receives only the disclosure classes explicitly granted for the specific scope requested; a grant on a proof record never implies a grant on the host payload, on signer identity attributes, on sensitive validation diagnostics or on any parent, sibling or referenced record.
exceptions: Public verifiability exception: where the owner package declares a proof publicly verifiable, the proof bytes, the verification method reference, the pinned method identifier and the certificate or public key may be disclosed publicly, while host content, signer identity attributes, revocation investigation detail and sensitive diagnostics remain closed under their own classes.

Compromise response exception: the responsible owner may grant time-boxed read of revocation evidence and frozen affected-scope lists to named responders, with a mandatory expiry recorded on the exception and an automatic lapse when the expiry passes.

Legal hold exception: the records authority may extend read to preservation counsel or a court-appointed party without altering any component's disclosure classification, recording the hold reference as the ground.
Reviewer exception: a reviewer or auditor may receive full validation diagnostics for a specific decision under review, limited to that decision's scope and expiring with the review.
audit_requirements: Every grant, denial, exception and disclosure-class change is emitted as an event to the externally owned audit model; this model stores only the audit entry reference and never the audit trail, its content or its integrity mechanism.

Exception grants must carry the approving role reference, the ground code and the expiry so an external auditor can reconcile them against audit entries without access to this model's payload classes.
Retention, tamper-evidence and disposition of audit entries are governed entirely by the audit model; nothing in this model extends, shortens or asserts audit retention.
A reconciliation key must be recorded on each review and access-relevant record so that external audit entries can be matched to governance records without duplicating either.

read_order: AGENTS.md at the package root, to obtain Name, Type, Registry ID, Owner and the four URLs, before any record is read or written.
Specification URL, to load the model boundary, in-scope and out-of-scope statements and the boundary notes, so target-owned concepts are not attempted locally.
Storage type URL, to learn the projection in use - JSON, YAML, Markdown, HTML, Git, MCP or MongoDB - while treating it as a projection of the canonical record graph rather than as semantics.
Interface URL, to learn the read, create, update and delete surface and the disclosure-class scoping applied to reads.
Processes URL, to learn the supersession, change-control, compromise-response, exception, review, classification and retention procedures and which external model owns each execution step.

Composition links and known relations, to resolve the required external models before instantiation; if the registered parent or a required reference target does not resolve, instantiation is blocked rather than defaulted.

coverage.claim: This structure covers the governance and control surface of the digital signature and proof mixin: the separation of governance state from externally reported cryptographic outcome, immutable correction by supersession, controlled change to signing method, key reference, trust-anchor set and pinned policy, emergency compromise response with frozen scope and reported outcomes, bounded exceptions with mandatory expiry and rollback, role separation with explicitly prohibited combinations, review and approval evidence distinct from the audit trail, independently classified disclosure of proof components, and retention, legal-hold, preservation and tombstone binding to externally owned obligations. It is grounded in signature validation and signature policy standards, PKI revocation semantics, key management and algorithm transition guidance, content-provenance signing practice, records management authority guidance and one jurisdictional trust-service regime pinned by reference. It does not claim completeness over cryptographic execution, trust-service operation or legal effect, all of which are deliberately external.

checklist.notes: Identity priority places the authoritative master-system identifier first, then a governed global identifier or IRI, then a locally minted UUID or ULID with the reason recorded. Dates, digests and paths are explicitly excluded as identifiers. External issuer identifiers are carried verbatim in their own namespace.

Governance state vocabulary with permitted transitions, append-only supersession, expiry, invalidation by compromise, bounded exception and forward-only rollback. In-place substantive mutation is prohibited; the state is kept separate from the reported cryptographic outcome.

Supersession chains with forward and back links and fork rejection, host-subject binding as a mixin, role-holder bindings by reference, and fourteen composition links that assign every operational neighbour concept to a target model.

RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z, offset-less values rejected. Event time is recorded separately from observation or ingestion time, and a trusted time-stamp token's asserted time is a third, source-attributed value. Effective intervals apply to pins, regimes, transition statuses and role assignments.

Every reported outcome, compromise declaration, policy pin and disposition carries an attributed source, a reporting party and a time. Reviewed inputs are captured with versions or digests as they stood at decision time; preserved evidence sets record the trust path and revocation data current at signing.

Nine distinct roles with a hard prohibition on one party holding signing authorization, key custody, verification-policy authority and legal-effect assessment together, plus recorded conflict declaration and compensating control where separation is impossible.

Reported indications and sub-indications are recorded as attributed observations against pinned constraints; validation execution is external and outcomes are never recomputed, edited or overridden locally. Exceptions tolerate a deficient outcome without altering it.

Deny by default across bundle, layer, finding and artifact scopes, with six independent disclosure classes and an explicit non-implication rule between proof-bytes access and host-content or signer-attribute access. Four bounded exception types each carry a ground and, where relevant, an expiry.

Retention schedule and legal-hold binding by reference, preservation obligation stated by profile reference, and a tombstone containing only identifier, supersession links, reason, reported time and authority. Deletion execution, backup expiry, audit retention and host deletion are assigned to external models; no schedule resolving means retain and flag.

Six alignments recorded as versioned references without conformance claims: AdES validation status vocabulary, signature policy structure, Data Integrity proof properties, C2PA claim-signature and update-manifest model, X.509 revocation reason codes, and the algorithm transition regime. Storage and interface are treated as projections throughout.

Each state transition, change, exception and review names the authorised role and the roles barred from acting, with delegation recorded by reference and the requesting role excluded from sole approval.

Referenced external compromise declarations, asserted invalidity time distinguished from revocation publication time, frozen blast radius with recorded exclusions, required actions mapped to owning models, and time-stamp or preserved-evidence mitigation determinations.

Signer identity attributes are held only as references; proof timing values and status endpoints are classified in their own right because they can reveal information about a controller; diagnostics are sensitive by default with a redaction rule.

Every exception carries a ground code, purpose limitation, compensating condition, approving authority, mandatory expiry and rollback condition, and never modifies the reported cryptographic outcome or the pinned policy.
Jurisdiction is modelled as a code plus regime reference plus effective interval, with an explicit prohibition on deriving a local legal-validity flag from a pinned regime.

No portable metric for proof or signature strength, assurance level or residual risk is defined, because no cited normative source supplies one that is transferable across signature families. Any local scoring would be unsupported structure and is deliberately omitted.
No coordinate, geometry or physical-location semantics apply to a proof record. Spatial reasoning is confined to jurisdiction as a legal-regime dimension, handled under spatial and jurisdiction.

known_omissions: The registered parent WM-XCT-006 is asserted from the registry entry alone. Its identity and semantics could not be verified against any external source, so the CHILD link rests on the sourced mixin-attachment pattern rather than on evidence about the parent itself, and should be treated as a gap until the parent specification resolves.

ETSI deliverables could not be retrieved directly through the fetch path used, which refused the ETSI document server. Their titles, versions and the specific definitions relied upon were corroborated from the ETSI deliverable listing and from European Commission DSS documentation. Any structure resting solely on ETSI text should be re-verified against the ETSI PDFs before adoption.

No portable measure of proof strength, cryptographic assurance level or residual risk is modelled; none of the cited sources defines one that transfers across X.509, Data Integrity and COSE-based signature families.

Selective-disclosure and unlinkable derived proofs are carried only as method identifiers. Their governance implications - in particular whether a derived proof supersedes, extends or is independent of its source proof - are not resolved here.
Multi-signature quorum policy, counter-signature ordering beyond linear proof chains, and threshold or multi-party signing arrangements are left to the host or workflow model.
Post-quantum migration dates are pinned by reference and not asserted, because the cited NIST transition documents were in draft status when accessed.
Hardware attestation of the signing environment and remote signing service assurance are referenced as method parameters but not modelled as their own governance surface.
Records management sources cited are US federal authority guidance; no equivalent non-US national records authority requirement was surveyed, so retention vocabulary may need regional substitution.
conflicts: Timestamp handling: Data Integrity permits proof timestamps without a timezone offset and treats them as UTC, whereas this model rejects offset-less values. The divergence is recorded as an alignment conflict; ingesting a Data Integrity proof requires the offset to be supplied or the value to be flagged as inferred.

Validation vocabularies do not have a normative crosswalk. AdES indications and sub-indications, C2PA error, warning and informational status codes, and Data Integrity verification results are structurally different. Any mapping between them is a local assertion that must be evidenced, not a conformance claim.

The X.509 superseded revocation reason applies to certificates, not to signatures or proofs. Reusing it as a supersession vocabulary for proof records is an analogy adopted for consistency, not conformance to RFC 5280 semantics.

Minimum evidence sets differ. C2PA treats a time-stamped manifest as remaining valid after credential expiry, while the NARA e-signature guidance requires retaining the certificates, the CRL current at signing and the trust path. Both are accommodated, but an adopting Dimension must choose which minimum it holds itself to and record that choice.

No cited standard defines revocation of a signature itself. Revocation attaches to certificates and keys. The model therefore records invalidation of the governance state plus references to external revocation evidence, and an implementer expecting a signature-revocation primitive will not find one.

FIPS 186-5 carries a published errata notice, so a pinned algorithm identifier should record the errata state; treating the base publication as the sole reference could pin a superseded parameter set.

Jurisdictional divergence is live: the UK-retained revised text of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 has diverged from the EU consolidated text and carries further pending amendments, so a regime reference without a jurisdiction code and effective interval is ambiguous.
regional_assumptions: Qualified electronic signature, seal, validation and preservation regimes derive from EU law and its retained national variants. They are pinned as references with jurisdiction and effective interval and are never treated as universal facts about a proof.

The UK-retained text of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 was used as the accessible authoritative rendering of the article structure. It is not identical to the current EU consolidated text and must not be substituted for it in an EU context.

NARA guidance binds US federal agencies. It is used here for its enumeration of the evidence needed to revalidate a signature over time and for retention and disposition separation, not as a globally applicable obligation.

CA/Browser Forum requirements bind publicly trusted code-signing certification authorities. They evidence industry-normative separation of key protection from CA operation and bounded revocation response; they are not general signature law and do not apply to private or enterprise trust domains.
NIST publications express US federal cryptographic transition policy. Other jurisdictions publish differing algorithm transition schedules, so transition status must always carry its source regime.
No assumption is made that a proof accepted in one jurisdiction carries legal effect in another; cross-border recognition is an external legal determination.
adversarial_checks: Tested whether any finding grants this model ownership of cryptographic verification. The state finding records only reported indications with attribution and time, no function performs validation, and the integrity rule explicitly forbids treating a locally computed digest as equivalent to an external validator's result.

Tested whether the retention finding implies deletion execution. The delete rules assign erasure, backup expiry, audit retention and host deletion to external models, and this model writes only a tombstone after disposition is reported to it; an unresolvable schedule causes retention and flagging rather than default disposal.

Tested whether role separation can silently collapse. The register requires distinct references for signing authorization, key custody, verification-policy authority and legal-effect assessment, and a single-party assignment must record an explicit conflict declaration, a compensating control, an approving role and a re-evaluation point.

Tested whether public verifiability leaks payload. Disclosure classes are independent and the access default rule states that a grant on proof bytes never implies a grant on host content, signer identity attributes or diagnostics; proof timing values and status endpoints are classified separately because they can themselves disclose controller information.

Rejected an attractive but unsupported signature-revocation primitive. No cited standard defines revocation of a signature; revocation attaches to certificates and keys, so the model records governance-state invalidation plus references to external revocation evidence, and this limitation is recorded as a conflict rather than papered over.

Rejected a local legal-validity flag. Legal effect under a qualified regime is jurisdictional and assessed externally, so only a pinned regime reference with jurisdiction code and effective interval is held, and a dedicated policy forbids deriving a validity conclusion from it.

Checked that no bundle reproduces an audit trail. Review and approval records hold decision evidence and an audit entry reference only; audit capture, storage, tamper-evidence and audit retention are assigned to the audit model, and the access requirements state that nothing here extends or asserts audit retention.

Checked that the compromise finding does not annex incident response. Declarations are issued externally, revocation and key destruction are executed by the key and PKI models, and this model records the reference, the frozen scope, the required actions with their owning models and the outcomes those models reported.

Checked that the change-control layer does not annex key rotation or policy authoring. The change function records an approved decision and its obligations, with policy authoring assigned to the signature-policy authority and key rotation to the cryptographic custodian in the key model.
